segments.english: They said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" He said, "Look, in the tent."
segments.literal: and-they-said to-him where Sarah your-wife and-he-said look in-the-tent

tokens.note: wayyiqtol (sequential imperfect), 3rd person masculine plural, of אמר
the noun is in the construct form before the suffix 2nd person masculine singular
wayyiqtol, 3rd person masculine singular

phrases.literal: and-they-said to-him; the vav is rendered by the sense of the sequence
where Sarah your-wife; the Hebrew has no verb, the English supplies 'is'
and-he-said; the speaker changes to the one who answers
look in-the-tent; the answer gives the place

grammar: The two wayyiqtol verbs (וַיֹּאמְרוּ, וַיֹּאמֶר) carry the narrative sequence: first the visitors speak, then the one addressed answers.
The question has no verb: אַיֵּה שָׂרָה אִשְׁתֶּךָ is 'where Sarah your wife', and the English supplies 'is'.
The etnaḥta on אִשְׁתֶּךָ closes the question; the silluq on בָאֹהֶל closes the verse.

The letters א, י and ו of אֵלָיו carry dots above them (puncta extraordinaria). Rashi and Radak, after Bereshit Rabbah, read the dotted letters as אַיּוֹ, 'where is he?': the visitors asked Sarah about Abraham too. The English reads the word as written, 'to him'.
segments.note: The answer 'in the tent' is taken as the modest place of a woman who stays inside (Rashi). The English states the place only.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the letters אי"ו of אֵלָיו are dotted. R. Shimon ben Elazar: where the undotted letters outnumber the dotted, one expounds the writing; where the dotted outnumber the undotted, one expounds the dots, and here they spell אַיּוֹ 'where is he?': they asked Sarah too where Abraham was. Hence a guest asks the man about the wife and the wife about the man. Bava Metzia: the angels knew where Sarah was, but asked to make known that she was modest and so endear her to her husband; R. Yose bar Ḥanina: to send her the cup of blessing. A midrash on the dots; the English reads 'to him' as written.
Rashi: the answer 'Look, in the tent' tells that she is modest (צְנוּעָה הִיא): she stays inside the tent. The English gives the place; the modesty is in this note.

apparatus: Puncta extraordinaria over the letters א, י, ו of אֵלָיו (WLC note 4). Rashi and Radak, citing R. Shimon ben Elazar (Bereshit Rabbah 48), read the dotted letters as אַיּוֹ, 'where is he?'.

segments.english: He said, "I will surely return to you at this time next year, with Sarah alive, and Sarah your wife will have a son." And Sarah was listening at the entrance of the tent, and he was behind it.
segments.literal: and-he-said return I-will-return to-you as-the-time living and-look son to-Sarah your-wife and-Sarah listening opening-of the-tent and-he behind-it

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, 3rd person masculine singular
infinitive absolute before the finite verb: emphasis, 'I will surely return'
yiqtol, 1st person common singular
כ + עֵת: the appointed season; Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as this season next year

feminine singular adjective without a noun. Ibn Ezra: of Sarah, 'alive' (as the greeting כֹּה לֶחָי, 1 Sam 25:6); Radak: Sarah as a woman giving birth (Mishnaic חַיָּה, 'woman in childbirth'); Onkelos and Rashi's second reading: of the time, 'when you are alive'. The lexicon's sense 3, 'reviving', takes the phrase of the season, the spring.
וְהִנֵּה presents the promised son as already in view; the English leaves it unrendered, as the decisions allow.
construct form with the 2nd person masculine singular suffix
qal participle, feminine singular, after its subject: a circumstantial clause, 'Sarah was listening'.
the personal pronoun as subject of a verbless clause: the visitor who speaks (Ibn Ezra). Rashi takes it of the entrance (masculine פֶּתַח).

the preposition אַחֲרֵי with the 3rd masculine singular suffix, 'behind it' or 'behind him'. Ibn Ezra: the speaker was behind the tent (masculine אֹהֶל); Rashi and Radak: the entrance was behind the speaker.

phrases.literal: and-he-said

phrases.english: I will surely return to you
phrases.literal: return I-will-return to-you; the infinitive absolute gives the emphasis

phrases.english: at this time next year, with Sarah alive
phrases.literal: as-the-time living: כָּ with the article, 'at this time'. Ibn Ezra: in the next year, and the feminine חַיָּה is Sarah, alive (ושרה חיה), like כֹּה לֶחָי (1 Sam 25:6). 'next year' and 'Sarah' are supplied from his reading

phrases.english: and Sarah your wife will have a son
phrases.literal: and-look son to-Sarah your-wife; וְהִנֵּה is left unrendered, and 'will have' is supplied in the verbless clause

phrases.english: and Sarah was listening at the entrance of the tent
phrases.literal: and-Sarah listening opening-of the-tent; the participle gives the continuing act

and-he behind-it: Ibn Ezra: 'he' is the angel who spoke with Abraham, behind the tent (masculine אֹהֶל), while Abraham sat at its entrance and did not see Sarah. Rashi and Radak: the entrance was behind the angel

grammar: The infinitive absolute שׁוֹב before the yiqtol אָשׁוּב is the emphatic form: 'I will surely return'.

כָּעֵת חַיָּה is an adverbial phrase: כְּ with the article, 'at the time', and the feminine adjective חַיָּה, 'living'. Ibn Ezra: this time next year, with Sarah alive; Radak: Sarah giving birth; Onkelos: 'when you are alive'.
וְהִנֵּה־בֵן לְשָׂרָה is verbless: 'and look, a son to Sarah'; the English supplies 'will have'.

The etnaḥta on אִשְׁתֶּךָ divides the verse: the promise, then the scene at the tent. Both clauses after it are circumstantial, a subject before a participle (וְשָׂרָה שֹׁמַעַת) and a pronoun before a preposition (וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו).
segments.note: Ibn Ezra reads כָּעֵת חַיָּה as 'at this time next year, with Sarah alive' (like כֹּה לֶחָי, 1 Sam 25:6); the English follows him and supplies 'next year' and Sarah's name from the feminine adjective. Rashi's second reading and Onkelos ('when you are alive') and Radak (Sarah giving birth) are in the commentary and the notes. In the last clause the English follows Ibn Ezra: 'he' is the visitor who speaks and 'it' the tent; Rashi and Radak read 'the entrance was behind him'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the angel does not promise his own return; he speaks on the errand of the Place (בִּשְׁלִיחוּתוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם), as in 16:10 where the angel says 'I will multiply', so the words are God's. The English keeps the first person of the speech.
Rashi: כָּעֵת is this season of the next year, which was Passover, and Isaac was born at the next Passover; the word is read כָּעֵת, not כְּעֵת. The English gives 'at this time next year'.
Rashi's second reading: 'this time' is a time that will be alive for you (שֶׁתְּהֵא חַיָּה לָכֶם), that you will all be whole and enduring. The English does not adopt it.
Rashi: הַפֶּתַח הָיָה אַחַר הַמַּלְאָךְ, the entrance was behind the angel; so Radak and Sforno. The English follows Ibn Ezra, 'he was behind it', and records this.

Ibn Ezra: 'at this time in the next year' (כעת הזאת בשנה האחרת), and חַיָּה is Sarah, alive (ושרה חיה), like the greeting כֹּה לֶחָי, 'so to the living' (1 Sam 25:6). The English follows: 'at this time next year, with Sarah alive'.

Ibn Ezra: 'he' is the angel who was speaking with Abraham; he was behind the tent, and Abraham, sitting at the entrance of the tent, did not see Sarah. Others say the entrance of Sarah's tent was behind Abraham's tent (וי"א פתח האהל שלה היה אחרי אהל אברהם). The English follows his first reading, 'he was behind it'.

context: Genesis pictures Abraham as a herdsman living in tents (12:8, 13:3, 18:1). Elsewhere in Genesis wives have tents of their own (24:67, 31:33), which is the picture behind the reading, given by Ibn Ezra, that Sarah's tent stood behind Abraham's.

segments.english: Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in days; Sarah had ceased to have the way of women.
segments.literal: and-Abraham and-Sarah old coming in-days; ceased to-be for-Sarah way as-women

tokens.note: qal participle of בּוֹא, 'come': 'come into days'
the plural of יוֹם in the sense 'days', with ב
qatal, 3rd person masculine singular; the subject is the custom of women
infinitive construct of היה, with ל: 'to be for her'
the way (custom) of women; the phrase is a euphemism for the monthly course
כ with the plural of אִשָּׁה

phrases.literal: and-Abraham and-Sarah; the vav is rendered 'now' as the start of the new clause
old coming in-days; 'advanced in days' is the reading of Ibn Ezra (reached many days)
ceased to-be for-Sarah; the verb takes the infinitive, and the subject is the matter of the verse

phrases.english: to have the way of women
phrases.literal: way as-women; 'the way of women' is the euphemism of Rashi's reading (the monthly course)

grammar: חָדַל לִהְיוֹת is 'ceased to be': a qatal of cessation with an infinitive construct; its subject is אֹרַח. Rashi glosses it as 'ceased from her'.
בָּאִים בַּיָּמִים is the idiom for old age: 'coming into days', the participle of בּוֹא with ב.
אֹרַח כַּנָּשִׁים is a noun phrase with כ of comparison: 'a way like women's'. The silluq on כַּנָּשִׁים closes the verse.
The etnaḥta on בַּיָּמִים divides the verse: the age of the couple, then the cessation in Sarah.
segments.note: The English 'the way of women' is the Hebrew's own euphemism. Rashi names it as the custom of the menstrual course; the English does not name it.

commentary.summary: Rashi: חָדַל לִהְיוֹת means פָּסַק מִמֶּנָה, it ceased from her. The English reads 'had ceased'.
Rashi: אֹרַח here is אֹרַח נִדּוֹת, the custom of the menstrual course. The English uses 'the way of women', the euphemism of the text, and does not name it.
Ibn Ezra: בָּאִים בַּיָּמִים means הגיעו לימים רבים, they reached many days. The English gives 'advanced in days'.

segments.english: Sarah laughed to herself, saying, "After I am worn out, shall I have delight, and my lord is old?"
segments.literal: and-she-laughed Sarah within-her-inward-part saying after my-being-worn-out she-was to-me delight and-my-lord old

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, 3rd person feminine singular
the inward part (קֶרֶב) with the 3rd feminine singular suffix; she laughed inwardly, not aloud
infinitive construct of אמר with ל, introducing speech; after בְּקִרְבָּהּ it is speech within herself (Radak: she thought it in her heart).
infinitive construct of בלה with 1st person singular suffix
qatal of היה read by Ibn Ezra as future: 'shall it be to me'
a feminine noun; Rashi's two other readings are in the commentary
my lord: Abraham as husband (a man), not God
qatal of זקן, 3rd person masculine singular

phrases.literal: and-she-laughed Sarah within-her; the laugh is inward (Ibn Ezra: בנפשה)
to-say
after my-being-worn-out
it-has-been to-me delight: Ibn Ezra reads the qatal as a future (כמו תהיה לי) and the words as a question, 'how shall delight be renewed for me?'
and-my-lord old

grammar: The verse has no interrogative particle; the question is Ibn Ezra's reading of Sarah's words: 'how shall the delight of youth be renewed for me?'.
The verb הָיְתָה is a qatal used for the future (Ibn Ezra: כמו תהיה לי); the English 'shall I have' gives that sense.
The verse turns on two clauses: 'after I am worn out' (the infinitive of בלה with the suffix) and 'my lord is old' (a qatal of זקן, with the subject אֲדֹנִי).
The wayyiqtol וַתִּצְחַק and the infinitive לֵאמֹר introduce the speech; after בְּקִרְבָּהּ it is said within herself, not aloud.
segments.note: עֶדְנָה is 'delight' (Ibn Ezra, and the lexicon). Rashi reads softness of flesh, and a second reading 'the time of the menstrual course'; both are recorded in the commentary.

commentary.summary: Rashi: she looked at her inward parts and said, 'Can these innards carry a child? Can these withered breasts give milk?' (Tanḥuma). He reads בְּקִרְבָּהּ of her body; the English follows Ibn Ezra, 'within herself', and records this midrash.

Rashi: עֶדְנָה is the softness or smoothing of the flesh (צִחְצוּחַ בָּשָׂר), and in a second reading the time of the menstrual course (זְמַן וֶסֶת נִדּוּת). The English takes 'delight' with Ibn Ezra and records these.
Ibn Ezra: הָיְתָה לִּי means תִּהְיֶה לִּי, shall it be to me. The English reads the qatal as 'shall I have'.

Ibn Ezra: עֶדְנָה is like עֵדֶן and עֹנֶג, delight and pleasure, as וַיִּתְעַדְּנוּ (Neh 9:25). The sense: after I am worn out and grown old, how shall the delight and pleasure of youth be renewed for me? And moreover (ועוד) my lord is old. The English gives 'delight'.
Ibn Ezra: בְּקִרְבָּהּ means within herself (בנפשה), and the LORD revealed her secret to the angel. The English gives 'to herself'.

context: Sarah calls her husband אֲדֹנִי, 'my lord', the respectful term of a woman for the man of her household (compare Judg 19:26–27); Hebrew also calls a husband בַּעַל, 'master'.

segments.english: The LORD said to Abraham, "Why is it that Sarah laughed, saying, 'Is it even true that I shall bear a child, now that I have grown old?'"
segments.literal: and-said the-LORD to Abraham why this laughed Sarah saying is-it-even truly I-shall-bear and-I have-grown-old

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, 3rd person masculine singular
לָמָּה: 'for what', the interrogative
enclitic זֶה after an interrogative gives the question force: 'why is it that'.
qatal, 3rd person feminine singular
infinitive construct of אמר with ל
the interrogative הֲ with אַף, 'even, also': Rashi and Radak gloss הֲגַם, 'is it even (true)'.
Ibn Ezra: the mem is an added letter, as the mem of שִׁלְשֹׁם; the base is אֹמֶן, 'truth'.
yiqtol, 1st person common singular, of ילד; Rashi reads it as 'shall I truly bear'
qatal, 1st person common singular; the words of Sarah 'my lord is old' are changed to 'I am old' (Rashi)

phrases.literal: and-he-said the-LORD
to Abraham

phrases.english: Why is it that Sarah laughed
phrases.literal: why this laughed Sarah: זֶה after the interrogative gives force, 'why is it that'
saying

phrases.english: Is it even true that I shall bear a child
phrases.literal: is-it-even truly I-shall-bear: Rashi and Radak gloss הֲגַם אֱמֶת; 'a child' is supplied

phrases.english: now that I have grown old
phrases.literal: and-I have-grown-old: Ibn Ezra, it renders her 'after I am worn out'

grammar: The LORD speaks in the wayyiqtol of the narrative, and the speech is direct: the double quotes are the LORD's words, and Sarah's words are inside them in single quotes.
לָמָּה זֶּה: the enclitic זֶה after the interrogative sharpens the question, 'why is it that'. The verb is a qatal (צָחֲקָה), the past reported to Abraham.
הַאַף אֻמְנָם: the interrogative הַ, אַף 'even', and אֻמְנָם 'truly', before the yiqtol אֵלֵד: 'is it even true that I shall bear?'.
The closing clause is a qatal, 1st person singular, וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי, where Sarah had said 'and my lord is old' (18:12).
segments.note: The LORD's words say 'I have grown old' where Sarah had thought 'after I am worn out ... and my lord is old' (18:12). Ibn Ezra: 'I have grown old' renders her 'after I am worn out', and the words are true. Rashi and Ramban add that 'my lord is old' was left out for the sake of peace. The English keeps the words as written.

commentary.summary: Rashi: הַאַף אֻמְנָם is הֲגַם אֱמֶת אֵלֵד, 'shall I truly, in truth, bear?'. The English reads 'Shall I truly bear a child'.
Rashi: Scripture changed Sarah's 'and my lord is old' to 'and I am old' for the sake of peace (מִפְּנֵי הַשָּׁלוֹם). The English keeps 'I am old'.

Ibn Ezra: וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי is the sense of her 'after I am worn out' (אחרי בלותי), and the angel spoke the truth: he reported what she said in other words. The English gives 'now that I have grown old'.
The word ומ"ם is the opening of the comment filed as ibn-ezra:18:13:3: 'and the mem [of אֻמְנָם] is added, as the mem of שִׁלְשֹׁם'. The anchoring split one sentence; its sense is given there.

Ibn Ezra: the mem of אֻמְנָם is added, as in שִׁלְשֹׁם (31:5). He then reports other commentators: the three men were prophets; to the objection that a prophet does not come to a prophet, they answer that the men came to Sarah (hence 'where is Sarah your wife'), and two went on to Sodom; on that reading 'they ate' is literal and אֲדֹנַי in 18:3 means 'my masters'. He gives further views on the order of the chapter and says no scribal correction is needed; his own view, he says, is hinted at in the portion of Shemot. The English 'truly' follows his first words.
Ramban: 'and I am old' is the sense of אחרי בלותי; the LORD's words are true, and out of regard for peace he did not repeat 'my lord is old'. The English agrees.

apparatus: Sarah's words 'and my lord is old' (18:12) and the LORD's 'and I have grown old' (18:13) differ; the English follows the words of each speaker, and the commentators' accounts are in the commentary.
The ibn-ezra:18:13:2 entry (ומ"ם) is the first word of the comment on אֻמְנָם filed as ibn-ezra:18:13:3; the anchoring has split one sentence in two.

segments.english: Is anything hidden from the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, at this time next year, with Sarah alive, and Sarah will have a son.
segments.literal: is-it-hidden from-the-LORD anything to-the-appointed-time I-will-return to-you as-the-time living and-to-Sarah son

tokens.note: nifal yiqtol, 3rd person masculine singular, with the interrogative ה; Rashi and Ibn Ezra read 'hidden' (היתכסי), which the lexicon does not list
the subject of the nifal: 'a matter'
לַמּוֹעֵד: the appointed time of 17:21 (Rashi)
yiqtol, 1st person common singular
כ + עֵת, as in 18:10
the feminine adjective, as in 18:10: Ibn Ezra takes it of Sarah, alive.

phrases.english: Is anything hidden from the LORD
phrases.literal: is-it-hidden from-the-LORD anything; the first clause is a question
to-the-appointed-time
I-will-return to-you

phrases.english: at this time next year, with Sarah alive
phrases.literal: as-the-time living: as in 18:10; 'next year' and 'Sarah' are supplied from Ibn Ezra's reading there

phrases.english: and Sarah will have a son
phrases.literal: and-to-Sarah son; the verb is supplied

grammar: הֲיִפָּלֵא is a question with the interrogative ה and a nifal yiqtol: 'is anything hidden from the LORD?'.
לַמּוֹעֵד, 'at the appointed time', is a noun with ל and the article: the time set in 17:21. כָּעֵת חַיָּה repeats the words of 18:10.
וּלְשָׂרָה בֵן is verbless: 'and to Sarah a son'; the English supplies 'will have'.
The etnaḥta on דָּבָר divides the verse: the question, then the promise repeated.
segments.note: Rashi and Ibn Ezra take הֲיִפָּלֵא as 'hidden' (היתכסי, היעלם), and the English follows them. The lexicon's Niph senses ('beyond one's power, difficult') are the other reading; Radak takes it so, and it is recorded.

commentary.summary: Rashi: הֲיִפָּלֵא is הֲיִתְכַּסִּי, 'is it concealed?' (as its Targum). Is any wondrous, separated or hidden thing hidden from me in doing my will? The English reads 'hidden from the LORD'.
Rashi: לַמּוֹעֵד is that appointed time that was set for you yesterday, at this time next year. The English gives 'at the appointed time' and 'at this time next year'.
Ibn Ezra: הֲיִפָּלֵא means היעלם, is hidden. Others say it means 'not a wonder for God', but then the mem would not be attached to the Name; he rejects that. The English follows 'hidden'.

Radak (not normative): things that seem strange to people are hidden from them, but nothing is hard for the LORD (לֹא יִפָּלֵא מִמֶּנּוּ דָּבָר). The English does not adopt this reading; it is recorded here.

apparatus: 18:14.2 vowels: WLC reads מֵיְהוָה; the base text reads מֵיְהֹוָה. The English is the same.

segments.english: Sarah denied, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. He said, "No, but you did laugh."
segments.literal: and-she-denied saying not I-laughed for she-was-afraid and-he-said no but you-laughed

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, Piel, 3rd person feminine singular: she acted deceptively
infinitive construct of אמר with ל
qatal, 1st person common singular
the first כִּי is causal, 'for' (Rashi)
qatal, 3rd person feminine singular
wayyiqtol, 3rd person masculine singular
the second כִּי means 'but' (אֶלָּא), as Rashi reads it

grammar: The first כִּי gives the reason for the denial ('for she was afraid'); the second corrects it ('no, but you did laugh'), as Rashi reads the two.
The wayyiqtol וַתְּכַחֵשׁ is piel, the denial; the two qatal forms (צָחַקְתִּי, יָרֵאָה) are the past of the speech.
The etnaḥta on יָרֵאָה closes the clause of the reason, and the silluq on צָחָקְתְּ closes the verse on the correction.
The English 'did laugh' supplies the auxiliary for the second person feminine qatal.
segments.note: Sarah's denial is a lie told out of fear (Radak); the LORD answers that she laughed. The English keeps both quotations in direct speech.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the first כִּי means 'for' (הָרִאשׁוֹן ... דְּהָא), giving the reason for the denial: she was afraid. The second means 'but' (אֶלָּא): 'No, but you did laugh'. The English follows both.

phrases.literal: and-Abraham going with-them to-escort-them: subject before participle, a circumstantial clause

grammar: Two wayyiqtol verbs (וַיָּקֻמוּ, וַיַּשְׁקִפוּ) carry the narrative; the subject הָאֲנָשִׁים stands after the first verb and its adverb.
וַיַּשְׁקִפוּ is the hiphil of שׁקף, 'look down' from a height; with עַל־פְּנֵי, 'over the face of', it is the view down over Sodom.
וְאַבְרָהָם הֹלֵךְ: subject before participle, a circumstantial clause, 'while Abraham was going with them'. The infinitive לְשַׁלְּחָם gives the purpose.
The piel of שׁלח, 'send off', is here seeing guests on their way (Rashi and Radak: לְלַוּוֹתָם).
segments.note: Rashi reads the verb of looking down as a look for evil; the English keeps the neutral 'looked down' and records this. Rashi reads לְשַׁלְּחָם as escort, as one who supposes they are guests.

commentary.summary: Rashi: every הַשְׁקָפָה in Scripture is for harm, except 'look down from your holy dwelling' (Deut 26:15), for great is the power of gifts to the poor, which turns the attribute of anger into mercy. The English keeps the neutral 'looked down'.
Rashi: לְשַׁלְּחָם means לְלַוּוֹתָם, to escort them, as one who supposes they are guests (כַּסָּבוּר אוֹרְחִים הֵם). The English reads 'to escort them'.

context: Genesis places Sodom in the plain of the Jordan near the Dead Sea (13:10–12, 14:3). Its site is disputed, at the south end of the sea or north of it in the Jordan plain, and has not been identified with certainty. From the hill country near Hebron the land falls steeply east to that basin, the picture of 'looked down' here and in 19:28.
